idiom_name: scalameta meta.Tree case-class extractor patterns with Tree.Transformer
implementation_notes: Scala's case classes and extractors are the pattern language: a rule is case Term.Apply(Term.Name("pred"), args) => ... over scalameta's meta.Tree, with alternative patterns, guards, bindings and sequence matches. Traversal belongs to Tree.Transformer (apply recurses when super.apply is called), to .traverse and .collect for read-only visits, and to .transform for a whole-tree rewrite - so the rule set states shapes and actions while the engine owns the walk. The compiler checks pattern types and arity, so an impossible pattern is a warning rather than a silent non-match, which is why this form is the default over quasiquote patterns. Use it for scalafix-style rules and custom tools over trees parsed by scalameta (Scala 2.13 and Scala 3 both parse).
pitfalls: Extractor patterns are positional: a rule written against the wrong constructor arity does not compile-match and falls through to the catch-all, so each pattern needs a fixture that proves it actually fires.

Transformer.apply recurses only when super.apply is called; forgetting it stops the walk below the first match, and calling super in the wrong position applies rules repeatedly until the result stops changing.
meta.Tree equality is structural and matches are easy to over-specify (Seq versus List in argument lists), so bind children and inspect them rather than spelling out the whole subtree.

variants.name: Quasiquote patterns over syntax trees (q-strings)
variants.implementation_notes: A quasiquote writes the tree pattern as valid Scala source: case q"$lhs + 0" => lhs binds the subexpression, ..$ splices sequences, and interpolators select the grammar (q for terms, t for types, p for patterns, cq and fq for clauses and for-enumerators). scalameta documents quasiquotes for both construction and deconstruction, and scala.reflect's quasiquotes - documented as a Scala 2 feature - do the same over compiler trees inside macros. It is the most readable way to state a shape that mirrors source syntax, and the scalameta guide explicitly warns that quasiquote patterns are easy to write in a way that produces unintended match errors; keep them for short source-shaped rules and use the default variant for long-lived rule sets.
pitfalls: A quasiquote pattern is parsed as source, so an unquoted literal matches more broadly than it looks (a constant hole binds any constant); bind the part and check it explicitly.

Deconstruction is macro-based and tied to a tree dialect: scalameta meta.Tree and scala.reflect universe.Tree are different types with different imports, and scala.reflect quasiquotes are documented as Scala 2 only.
Splicing with ..$ is only valid where the grammar allows a sequence, so a splice in the wrong position either fails to compile or silently matches nothing.
